scenes.text: So, how effective is Australia's healthcare system, and for whom? Before we start, what would you measure to decide whether a healthcare system is working? Pick three things. Now, would any of your three notice a system that treats people brilliantly once they arrive, but that a tenth of the population can't reach?

A healthcare system is all the organisations, workers, funding and rules that deliver health services. It has six roles, and most people only picture the first. Treating illness and injury. Preventing illness and finding it early. Managing chronic conditions, now its biggest workload, and the one it was least built for. Rehabilitation, so treatment turns back into a life. Protecting people from financial hardship, because a system that cures you and bankrupts you has failed. And public health: tracking disease, controlling outbreaks, and regulating medicines and safety. So before you judge it, name the role. Judge it only on treatment, and it will always look good, because you've picked the test it passes.

Now judge each role in turn, because the verdicts differ, and that's the finding. Treatment is strong: survival from major conditions compares well, and avoidable deaths are below the wealthy-country average. Universal coverage means cost blocks fewer people from a GP or a hospital bed, and medicines are subsidised. Public health is strong too, from immunisation to tobacco control. But prevention gets a small share of spending, in a system that pays for activity, not for illness avoided. Chronic care is split into separate visits and separate conditions. Dental care and much allied and psychological care sit largely outside universal coverage. And split federal and state responsibilities leave gaps people fall through. Say only the strengths and it's a brochure. Only the weaknesses, and it's a complaint. And effective isn't the same as efficient, which is outcome for the money.

Then the question of for whom. Access means whether you can actually get care when you need it, and equity of access means people with the same need can get the same care, wherever they live and whoever they are. Year 11's access gates regroup into five. Availability: does the service exist, with room to see you? Affordability: what's left to pay, including travel and time off work? Accessibility: can you get there, and get in? Acceptability: would you go, given language, culture and past experience? And appropriateness: does it meet the need you actually have? The gates are in series. Pass four and fail one, and you get no care. And you can see the failures in the data, because outcomes still follow postcode.

The syllabus names three places to improve. In rural and remote areas: telehealth, wider roles for nurses, pharmacists and rural generalists, rural training that keeps doctors local, and better retrieval. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples: growing community-controlled services and their funding, growing the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health workforce, measuring cultural safety from the patient's side, and letting communities decide service design. For people with disability: removing physical and communication barriers, training clinicians not to blame every new symptom on the disability, and joining health and disability support. And one opportunity runs through all three: continuity of care, being seen over time by someone who knows you. That's what a system paid by the visit does worst.

So how do you write "assess the effectiveness" well? Four moves. State the criterion, for example, the system's six roles. Give evidence both ways, in trends, not figures. Explain a trade-off, instead of listing. Why is prevention underfunded? Because the system pays for activity, the benefits arrive after the funding cycle, and an illness prevented is invisible. Then judge, with a qualifier. Effective at treating illness for most Australians, much less effective at prevention and at reaching some groups, and the second matters more, because the people it misses have the greatest need.
Two things to remember. Name the role before you judge it. And access is five gates in series.

Two exam questions. First. Case one: a patient's appointment is free, but they don't fill the prescription, because the medicine isn't subsidised and the pharmacy is a bus trip away. Case two: a man goes to emergency four times in a year for the same chronic condition, and each time he's treated and sent home. For each, name the gate that failed and one fix. Pause here to answer.

Case one fails affordability, the unsubsidised medicine, and accessibility, the bus trip. A fix: subsidise the medicine, or deliver it. Case two passes the first four gates every time, but fails appropriateness. Each visit treats the episode, not the condition. A fix: a regular GP who manages the condition over time. You could also argue availability, if he has no regular GP, and the fix is the same. The classic mistake is calling case two good access because he got in.
Second. A politician says Australia's healthcare system is highly effective, because hospital survival after heart attacks is among the best in the world. Assess this claim. Pause here to answer.

The claim is true for one role and silent on the rest. Hospital survival measures treatment, so it picks the test the system passes. Judged on all six roles, the system is strong at treatment, weaker at prevention and chronic care, and uneven in who gets in. So: effective at treatment, not yet effective for everyone. The classic mistake is accepting a verdict with no criterion.

So name the role, judge each one, test all five gates, and look for continuity. Now step through the hospital doors. Behind them are many doors, each paid for and run by someone different. Who actually runs health in Australia?
